title: Week 3 · Lesson 7: Hemodynamics, Edema, Thrombosis & Shock — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 3 — Lesson 7: Hemodynamics, Edema, Thrombosis & Shock

FNP-level goal: Connect hemodynamics to organ perfusion, recognize edema and thrombotic mechanisms, and identify shock before irreversible cellular injury develops.

Learning Objectives

  • Use CO = HR × SV and MAP ≈ CO × SVR clinically.
  • Apply preload, afterload, and contractility to heart failure and shock.
  • Build a mechanism-based edema differential.
  • Apply Virchow’s triad to VTE risk.
  • Recognize hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive, and obstructive shock.

Part 1 — Perfusion Is the Endpoint

The cardiovascular system must deliver oxygenated blood to tissue. Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate × stroke volume. A useful approximation is MAP ≈ CO × systemic vascular resistance (SVR).

Stroke volume is influenced by preload (filling), afterload (resistance to ejection), and contractility (myocardial force generation).

Numbers alone do not equal perfusion. Ask whether the brain, kidneys, skin, and other organs are receiving adequate flow.

Part 2 — Preload, Afterload, Contractility

Preload: ventricular filling before systole. Reduced intravascular volume lowers preload; excess volume can worsen congestion.

Afterload: pressure/resistance against which the ventricle ejects. Hypertension and vasoconstriction raise LV afterload.

Contractility: intrinsic myocardial pump strength. MI, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, and severe arrhythmia can reduce contractility.

MI → contractility ↓ → SV ↓ → CO ↓ → tissue perfusion ↓.

Part 3 — Edema Is a Mechanism Problem

Fluid movement reflects hydrostatic pressure, plasma oncotic pressure, vascular permeability, and lymphatic drainage.

  • Hydrostatic pressure ↑: heart failure, venous obstruction, venous hypertension.
  • Oncotic pressure ↓: hypoalbuminemia from nephrotic protein loss, advanced liver disease, or severe malnutrition.
  • Permeability ↑: inflammation, burns, allergic reactions, sepsis.
  • Lymphatic obstruction: malignancy, node removal, radiation, or other lymphatic injury.

Edema is a sign, not a diagnosis. Determine symmetry, onset, distribution, dyspnea/orthopnea, weight change, medication history, renal/hepatic/cardiac context, venous findings, and thrombotic risk.

Part 4 — Thrombosis and Virchow’s Triad

Virchow’s triad: endothelial injury + abnormal blood flow (especially stasis) + hypercoagulability.

Immobility, surgery, malignancy, estrogen exposure, pregnancy/postpartum state, prior VTE, inflammatory disease, and inherited/acquired prothrombotic states alter risk. VTE assessment combines symptoms, probability, risk factors, and an appropriate diagnostic pathway—not calf tenderness alone.

Part 5 — DVT to PE

Venous thrombus → embolization → pulmonary artery obstruction → V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia, RV afterload ↑, and possible reduced LV filling/CO.

PE can range from mild symptoms to obstructive shock. Acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, unexplained tachycardia, hypoxemia, or hypotension require urgent assessment in the correct clinical context.

Part 6 — Shock: Inadequate Tissue Perfusion

Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery/utilization leading to cellular dysfunction and organ injury. Early compensated shock can exist before profound hypotension.

Look for altered mental status, tachypnea, tachycardia, cool/mottled or sometimes warm skin, weak pulses, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, hypotension, metabolic acidosis/hyperlactatemia when measured, and a concerning trajectory.

Part 7 — Four Mechanisms of Shock

Hypovolemic: volume loss—hemorrhage, GI loss, dehydration, third spacing. Preload falls.

Cardiogenic: pump failure—MI, severe HF, myocarditis, arrhythmia, acute valve disease. Contractility/forward flow fail; congestion may coexist.

Distributive: pathologic vasodilation/permeability—sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic states. SVR falls and effective circulating volume is inadequate.

Obstructive: mechanical impediment—massive PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax. Forward flow is blocked.

Mixed shock occurs; for example, sepsis in a patient with chronic HF. Do not force every unstable patient into one pure category.

Part 8 — FNP Initial Assessment and Disposition

In an unstable patient, rapidly assess ABCs, vital signs, mental status, oxygenation, skin/perfusion, urine-output history, bleeding/infection/chest symptoms, medications, and relevant risk factors. Activate emergency services/ED transfer when shock, sepsis, massive PE, acute coronary syndrome, anaphylaxis, major bleeding, or another time-sensitive cause is possible.

The FNP role is mechanism-based recognition and escalation—not prolonged outpatient differentiation of shock.

Part 9 — Board-Style Case 1

A patient with melena, HR 128, BP 86/50, dizziness, cool skin, and low urine output has inadequate perfusion.

Mechanism: likely intravascular volume loss → preload ↓ → SV/CO ↓ → hypovolemic shock.

Decision: emergency evaluation for hemorrhage/resuscitation; do not manage as routine anemia follow-up.

Part 10 — Board-Style Case 2

A patient with recent surgery has sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and syncope.

Mechanism: possible PE with pulmonary vascular obstruction and RV strain.

Decision: emergency evaluation; do not dismiss this as anxiety or uncomplicated postoperative deconditioning.

FNP High-Yield Framework

CO = HR × SV; MAP ≈ CO × SVR.

Edema: hydrostatic pressure, oncotic pressure, permeability, lymphatic drainage.

VTE: endothelial injury + stasis + hypercoagulability.

Shock: volume, pump, vascular tone, or obstruction.

FNP decision: assess end-organ perfusion and trajectory; identify the most dangerous mechanism; escalate immediately for instability.
